name: Peru
seoTitle: History of Peru: Cradle of the Inca Empire, Red-White-Red Flag, and 1821 Independence
metaDescription: Discover the detailed history of Peru. Explore the Inca Empire of Cusco, Machu Picchu, José de San Martín's 1821 Independence, and the Peruvian flag.
mapFormation:
Spanning 1.28 million square kilometers along the central Pacific coast of South America, the Republic of Peru (Perú) encompasses three distinct geographic zones: the arid coastal desert (Costa), the towering Andean cordillera (Sierra) with peaks exceeding 6,700 meters, and the immense Amazonian rainforest basin (Selva) covering 60% of national territory.

Peru is the ancient home of Caral-Supe (c. 3000 BCE)—the oldest known civilization in the Americas—followed by the Chavín, Nazca, Moche, and Wari cultures. In the 15th century, the Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu) expanded from its capital in Cusco under Pachacuti, constructing monumental stone citadels like Machu Picchu and a 40,000-kilometer paved road network (Qhapaq Ñan).

Following the Spanish conquest led by Francisco Pizarro in 1532, Lima was founded in 1535 as the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru, the supreme administrative and mining center of the Spanish Empire in South America for nearly three centuries. Sovereign independence was proclaimed on July 28, 1821, by General José de San Martín, and finalized at the Battle of Ayacucho in 1824.
flagHistory:
The national flag of Peru—the Bandera Nacional—is a striking vertical triband of red, white, and red, designed by liberating general José de San Martín in 1820 and standardized by Congress on February 25, 1825.

According to historical tradition, while resting near the bay of Paracas, San Martín was inspired by a flock of parihuanas (flamingos with vivid red wings and white chests) soaring into the sky. In patriotic symbolism: Red honors the blood spilled by Inca warriors and patriot heroes defending the homeland; while White represents peace, justice, and social purity.

The state ensign (Pabellón Nacional) bears the National Shield in the white stripe, divided into three fields showcasing Peru's natural wealth: the Vicuña (animal kingdom), the Cinchona Tree (plant kingdom / source of quinine), and the Cornucopia spilling golden coins (mineral kingdom).
freedomStory:
Peru was the central stronghold of Spanish royalist power in South America, making its liberation a momentous continental campaign.

Following his legendary crossing of the Andes and liberation of Chile, General José de San Martín landed his liberating expedition at Paracas in 1820. On July 28, 1821, San Martín stepped onto the balcony of the Plaza Mayor in Lima and proclaimed the immortal words: 'From this moment on, Peru is free and independent by the general will of the peoples and by the justice of its cause that God defends. Long live the Homeland! Long live Freedom!'

Sovereign liberation across the continent was sealed on December 9, 1824, on the high Andean plateau at the Battle of Ayacucho, where Marshal Antonio José de Sucre decisively defeated the Spanish Viceroy, permanently ending three centuries of Spanish imperial rule in South America.
challenges: As a top global producer of copper, zinc, silver, and gold, Peru balances mining resource export growth with social development and environmental protection. Foremost priorities include strengthening democratic institutional stability, modernizing Andean irrigation and transport corridors, and protecting the Amazon biosphere against illegal gold mining.

faqs.question: When did Peru declare independence?
faqs.answer: Independence was proclaimed on July 28, 1821, by General José de San Martín in Lima, celebrated as Peru's National Day (Fiestas Patrias).

faqs.question: What is the historical significance of the Battle of Ayacucho (1824)?
faqs.answer: Fought on December 9, 1824, the Battle of Ayacucho was the final major military engagement of the Spanish American wars of independence, ending Spanish colonial rule in South America.

timeline.event: The Sacred City of Caral-Supe develops as the oldest known civilization in the Americas.
Pachacuti expands the Inca Empire from Cusco, constructing Machu Picchu.
Francisco Pizarro founds the City of Kings (Lima) as the capital of the Viceroyalty.
General José de San Martín proclaims Peruvian independence in Lima on July 28.
The Battle of Ayacucho seals sovereign independence for Peru and South America.
Hiram Bingham brings international academic attention to the Inca citadel of Machu Picchu.
